content.text: Have you ever walked across a carpet and then felt a small shock when you touched a metal door handle? Or noticed your hair standing on end after pulling off a woollen jumper? These everyday experiences are caused by
— electric charge that builds up on the surface of objects and stays in place rather than flowing as a current.

Static electricity is one of the oldest observed electrical phenomena. The ancient Greeks discovered that rubbing amber with fur would cause the amber to attract small objects like feathers and dust. In fact, the word "electricity" comes from the Greek word
, meaning amber. Understanding static electricity is fundamental to understanding how charge behaves, how electric fields work, and how many modern technologies operate.
In this lesson, we will explore how objects become charged, the forces between charges, electric fields and field lines, and both the dangers and practical uses of static electricity.
All matter is made up of atoms, and atoms contain three types of subatomic particles:
— positively charged particles found in the nucleus
— neutral particles (no charge) found in the nucleus
— negatively charged particles that orbit the nucleus
In a neutral atom, the number of protons equals the number of electrons, so the overall charge is zero. An object becomes electrically charged when it gains or loses electrons.

Different materials have different tendencies to gain or lose electrons. This tendency is described by the

(also called delocalised electrons) that are not tightly bound to any particular atom and can move freely through the material. Examples include copper, aluminium, silver, and gold.
are materials that do not allow charge to flow through them easily. Their electrons are tightly bound to atoms and cannot move freely. Examples include plastic, rubber, glass, wood, and dry air.

is a device used to detect electric charge. It consists of:
A metal rod (or stem) connected to the cap
A thin gold leaf attached to the bottom of the rod
A glass case to protect the gold leaf from air currents

When a charged object is brought near (or touches) the metal cap, charge is distributed along the rod and the gold leaf. Since the rod and the leaf receive the same type of charge, they repel each other, causing the gold leaf to rise. The greater the charge, the more the leaf rises.
The electroscope can be used to:
— if the leaf rises, the object is charged.
— a larger charge causes a greater deflection.
Determine the sign of a charge
— by first charging the electroscope with a known charge and then bringing the test charge near it. If the leaf rises further, the test charge is the same sign; if it falls, it is the opposite sign.
The fundamental law of electrostatics states:
— two positive charges or two negative charges push each other away.
— a positive charge and a negative charge pull each other together.
This is the only reliable test for whether an object is charged. A charged object can attract both charged and uncharged objects (because it can induce a charge on a neutral object), but
repulsion only occurs between two objects carrying the same type of charge
. Therefore, repulsion is the definitive test for charge.

When a charged object is brought near a neutral conductor, the free electrons in the conductor are either attracted towards or repelled away from the charged object. This redistribution of charge is called
For example, if a negatively charged rod is brought near a neutral metal sphere:
The free electrons in the sphere are repelled to the far side of the sphere.
The near side of the sphere becomes positively charged (due to a deficit of electrons).
The far side becomes negatively charged (due to an excess of electrons).
The sphere is still neutral overall, but the charge has been redistributed. This induced charge separation explains why a charged object can attract small neutral objects like pieces of paper.

Static electricity can be dangerous in several situations:
When a large amount of static charge builds up, it can suddenly discharge as a
. This spark can ignite flammable materials. Dangerous situations include:

: Fuel flowing through pipes can cause static charge to build up. A spark near fuel vapour could cause an explosion. This is why aircraft are earthed (grounded) with a wire before refuelling, and why you should touch the metal of your car before handling the fuel nozzle.
: Sparks could ignite anaesthetic gases. Staff wear antistatic clothing and shoes, and floors are made of antistatic material.
: Fine dust particles in the air can be ignited by a static spark, causing a devastating explosion.
is a dramatic example of static discharge. During a thunderstorm:
Strong air currents cause ice crystals and water droplets inside clouds to collide and rub against each other.
This friction causes charge separation: the top of the cloud becomes positively charged, and the bottom becomes negatively charged.
The negatively charged base of the cloud induces a positive charge on the ground below.
When the potential difference between the cloud and the ground (or between two clouds) becomes large enough, the air breaks down and a massive spark — lightning — occurs.
Lightning conductors (lightning rods) on tall buildings provide a safe path for the charge to flow to earth, protecting the building from damage.
Despite its dangers, static electricity has many practical applications:
Power stations and factories that burn fossil fuels produce smoke containing tiny particles of ash and soot. An
removes these particles before the smoke leaves the chimney:
Smoke passes through a metal grid (or wires) connected to a high negative voltage.
The particles of ash and soot pick up negative charges from the grid.
The negatively charged particles are then attracted to positively charged collecting plates.
The particles stick to the plates and are periodically removed by tapping the plates.
The clean gas exits through the chimney.
This technology significantly reduces air pollution.
In spray painting (of cars, bicycles, and other objects):
The paint droplets are given a charge (usually negative) as they leave the spray nozzle.
The object to be painted is given the opposite charge (or is earthed/grounded).
The charged paint droplets are attracted to the object and spread out evenly over the surface, including around edges and into recesses.
Since all the paint droplets have the same charge, they repel each other, ensuring an even coat.
This method wastes less paint and gives a more uniform finish than conventional spraying.
Photocopiers use static electricity to produce copies of documents:
A drum inside the photocopier is given a uniform positive charge.
An image of the document is projected onto the drum. Where light hits the drum, the charge leaks away, leaving a pattern of charge that matches the dark areas of the document.
Negatively charged toner (fine black powder) is attracted to the positively charged areas of the drum.
A positively charged sheet of paper attracts the toner from the drum.
The paper is heated to fuse the toner permanently onto the paper.
Laser printers work on a similar principle, but a laser beam is used to create the charge pattern on the drum.
Similar to precipitators, electrostatic charge is used in some air purifiers and cleaners to attract and capture dust particles.

) is the process of connecting a charged object to the earth (ground) using a conductor. The Earth is so large that it can absorb or supply almost any amount of charge without becoming noticeably charged itself. It effectively acts as an infinite reservoir of charge.
When a negatively charged object is earthed:
Excess electrons flow from the object, through the conductor, and into the ground.
When a positively charged object is earthed:
Electrons flow from the ground, through the conductor, and into the object.
Earthing is used as a safety measure in many situations:
Fuel tankers have earthing chains or straps that drag along the ground to prevent charge build-up.
Electronic components can be damaged by static discharge. Technicians wear antistatic wrist straps connected to earth when handling sensitive components.
Metal cases of electrical appliances are earthed via the earth wire in the mains plug to prevent electric shock.

Explain why a charged balloon sticks to a neutral wall.

When the charged balloon (say, negatively charged) is placed against the wall, it repels electrons in the surface of the wall, pushing them deeper into the wall. This leaves the surface of the wall nearest to the balloon with a net positive charge (electrostatic induction). Since the negatively charged balloon is very close to the positively charged surface of the wall, the attractive force between them is strong enough to hold the balloon in place against gravity. The repulsive force from the negative charges deeper in the wall is weaker because they are farther away.
Describe how an electrostatic precipitator removes pollutant particles from smoke.

Smoke from the factory or power station enters the precipitator and passes through a metal grid or set of wires connected to a negative high-voltage supply. The smoke particles gain negative charges from the grid. The negatively charged smoke particles are then attracted towards positively charged collecting plates on the sides of the chimney. The particles accumulate on these plates and are periodically removed by mechanical hammering or rapping. The cleaned gas then exits through the top of the chimney. This process can remove over 99% of particulate matter from the exhaust gases.
This is incorrect. Charging by friction does not create charge. It simply transfers electrons from one object to another. The total charge of the system remains constant (conservation of charge).
Protons are fixed in the nucleus and do not move from one object to another during charging by friction. Only electrons are transferred.
"A charged object only attracts other charged objects."
A charged object can attract neutral objects through electrostatic induction. However, a charged object can only
another object if both carry the same type of charge. Repulsion is the definitive test for charge.
"Static electricity and current electricity are different types of electricity."

They both involve the same electric charges (electrons). The difference is that in static electricity, charges accumulate on surfaces, while in current electricity, charges flow continuously through a conductor.

While tall objects are more likely to be struck, lightning can strike anywhere. Lightning tends to follow the path of least resistance to the ground, which often (but not always) involves tall, pointed, or metallic objects.

In fact, insulators are easier to charge by friction precisely because charge stays where it is placed and does not flow away. Conductors can also be charged, but the charge must be prevented from leaking away (e.g., by insulating the conductor from the ground).

Describe and explain what happens to the gold leaf when a charged polythene rod is brought near the cap without touching.

The negatively charged polythene rod repels free electrons in the metal cap downward along the rod and onto the gold leaf. Both the rod (stem) and the gold leaf become negatively charged. Since they carry the same charge, they repel each other and the gold leaf rises. The closer the rod is brought, the more the leaf deflects. If the rod is removed, the electrons redistribute evenly and the leaf falls back down.
Explain why static charge build-up is dangerous during aircraft refuelling and describe one precaution.

As fuel flows through pipes and nozzles, friction between the fuel and the pipe walls can cause a build-up of static charge. If enough charge accumulates, a spark could occur. Since the area contains highly flammable fuel vapour, the spark could ignite the vapour and cause an explosion.
The aircraft is connected to earth (grounded) using a conducting wire or strap before refuelling begins, so that any charge that builds up flows safely to earth instead of accumulating.
Explain how giving the paint droplets a charge produces an even coat.
The paint droplets are all given the

charge (e.g., negative). Since like charges repel, the droplets spread out evenly and do not clump together. The object to be painted is earthed or given the opposite charge, so the charged droplets are attracted towards it, including into recesses and around edges. This results in an even, uniform coat with less waste.
Draw the electric field lines between two parallel plates.

See the ASCII diagram above (Uniform Field Between Parallel Plates). The field lines are straight, parallel, and equally spaced, running from the positive plate to the negative plate. The direction of the field is from positive to negative.
Explain the difference between a conductor and an insulator in terms of atomic structure, with examples.
have free (delocalised) electrons that are not tightly bound to atoms and can move freely through the material, allowing charge to flow easily. Examples: copper, aluminium.
have all their electrons tightly bound to atoms; there are no free charge carriers, so charge cannot flow. Examples: plastic, rubber.
Explain why a negatively charged rod attracts a neutral piece of aluminium foil.

The negatively charged rod repels free electrons in the foil to the far side (electrostatic induction). The near side of the foil becomes positively charged (deficit of electrons), and the far side becomes negatively charged (excess of electrons). The attractive force between the negative rod and the positive near side is stronger than the repulsive force between the rod and the negative far side (because the near side is closer), so there is a net attractive force.
Describe how a lightning conductor protects a building.

A lightning conductor is a thick copper strip running from a metal spike at the top of the building down to a metal plate buried in the ground. During a thunderstorm, if lightning strikes, the lightning conductor provides a low-resistance path for the huge current to flow safely to earth, rather than passing through the building structure. The pointed spike also helps to gradually discharge the charge build-up in the atmosphere above the building, reducing the likelihood of a strike.
Explain the role of static electricity in transferring toner to paper in a photocopier.

A rotating drum is given a uniform positive charge. An image of the document is projected onto the drum; light areas lose their charge while dark areas retain it, creating a charge pattern matching the original. Negatively charged toner powder is then attracted to the positively charged (dark) areas of the drum. A sheet of paper is given a stronger positive charge, which attracts the negatively charged toner from the drum onto the paper. Finally, the paper is heated to fuse (melt) the toner permanently onto it.
